Notation and conventions.
     • We use the standard abbreviations usc for ‘upper semicontinuous’, lsc for ‘lower
       semicontinuous’, wlog for ‘without loss of generality”, and iff for ‘if and only if’.
       We also use PL for ‘piecewise linear’, snc for ‘simple normal crossing’, and psh for
       ‘plurisubharmonic’.
     • Following the Bourbaki convention, all compact and locally compact topological
       spaces are required to be Hausdorff.
     • A net in a set X is a family (xi )i∈I of elements of X indexed by a directed set, i.e.
       a partially preordered set in which any two elements are dominated by a third one.
       A subnet of (xi )i∈I is a net of the form (xϕ(j) )j∈J where ϕ : J → I is increasing and
       final, i.e. for each i ∈ I there exists j ∈ J with ϕ(j) ≥ i. A (Hausdorff) topological
       space X is compact iff every net in X admits a convergent subnet.
     • If X is a Hausdorff topological space, and ϕ : X → R ∪ {±∞} is any function, then
       the usc regularization ϕ? of ϕ is the smallest usc function with ϕ? ≥ ϕ. Concretely,
       ϕ? (x) = lim supy→x ϕ(y). The lsc regularization is defined by ϕ? = −(−ϕ)? .
     • We work over an algebraically closed field k, for the most part of arbitrary charac-
       teristic. In this paper, a variety (over k) is a separated k-scheme of finite type that
       is reduced, but not necessarily irreducible, nor even equidimensional.
 10                      SÉBASTIEN BOUCKSOM AND MATTIAS JONSSON

     • For any variety X, we denote by Pic(X) the Picard group of isomorphism classes of
       line bundles. Elements of the associated Q-vector space Pic(X)Q := Pic(X) ⊗Z Q
       can be viewed as isomorphism classes of Q-line bundles.
     • If X is a projective variety, we denote by N1 (X) the finite dimensional R-vector
       space of numerical classes of R-Cartier divisors on X. It comes with a surjective
       linear map Pic(X)R → N1 (X) induced by L 7→ c1 (L) .
     • Ample classes form a nonempty open convex cone Amp(X) ⊂ N1 (X), whose closure
       is the closed convex cone Nef(X) ⊂ N1 (X) of nef classes. For θ, θ0 ∈ N1 (X), we
       write θ ≥ θ0 if θ − θ0 is nef. We generally denote by θ an element of N1 (X), and by
       ω an element of Amp(X).
     • The cone Psef(X) ⊂ N1 (X) of pseudoeffective classes is defined as the closed convex
       cone generated by classes of effective R-Cartier divisors; its interior Big(X) is the
       cone of big classes.
     • A section of a line bundle on X is regular if it does not vanish identically along any
       irreducible component of X. Its zero scheme is then a Cartier divisor on X.

           Definition 2.18). This set is non-empty iff L is effective.
  Given any numerical class θ ∈ N1 (X), we are seeking to define a class PSH(θ) of θ-
  plurisubharmonic functions (θ-psh functions for short) ϕ : X an → R ∪ {−∞}. By analogy
  with the complex analytic setting, these functions should be usc and generically finite, and
  the following properties should hold:
                                                gf
 (PSH1) for any L ∈ Pic(X)Q , we have HR           (L) ⊂ PSH(L) := PSH(c1 (L));
 (PSH2) if a generically finite function ϕ : X an → R ∪ {−∞} arises as the pointwise limit of
           a decreasing net (ϕi ) with ϕi ∈ PSH(θi ) and limi θi = θ, then ϕ ∈ PSH(θ).
  Note that (PSH2) implies the following two properties:
(PSH2a) for any function ϕ : X an → R ∪ {−∞}, the set of θ ∈ N1 (X) such that ϕ ∈ PSH(θ)
           is closed (possibly empty);
(PSH2b) for any θ ∈ N1 (X), the set PSH(θ) is closed under decreasing limits (provided the
           limit function is generically finite).

  tion:

  generically finite, usc function that can be written as the pointwise limit of a decreasing net

Lemma 4.3. For functions in PL(X)R , Definition 4.1 is consistent with Definition 3.2.

we get, in particular,

which provides a converse to (4.2).
Remark 4.4. If L is a Q-line bundle, then functions in PSH(L) = PSH(c1 (L)) can be
interpreted as psh metrics on L, using the trivial metric. By (4.3), any nef line bundle L

with the complex analytic case, where a nef and big line bundle may not admit any bounded
psh metric (see [BEGZ10, Example 5.4], based on [DPS94, Example 1.7]).

are satisfied.

L22: 【8†Proposition 29.28.1 (Generic flatness).】 Let $f : X \to S$ be a morphism of schemes. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a quasi-coherent sheaf of $\mathcal{O}_ X$-modules. Assume
L23: 
L24:   1. $S$ is integral,
L25: 
L26:   2. $f$ is of finite type, and
L27: 
L28:   3. $\mathcal{F}$ is a finite type $\mathcal{O}_ X$-module.
L29: 
L30: Then there exists an open dense subscheme $U \subset S$ such that $X_ U \to U$ is flat and of finite presentation and such that $\mathcal{F}|_{X_ U}$ is flat over $U$ and of finite presentation over $\mathcal{O}_{X_ U}$.
L31: Proof. As $S$ is integral it is irreducible (see Properties, Lemma 【14†28.3.4】) and any nonempty open is dense. Hence we may replace $S$ by an affine open of $S$ and assume that $S = \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(A)$ is affine. As $S$ is integral we see that $A$ is a domain. As $f$ is of finite type, it is quasi-compact, so $X$ is quasi-compact. Hence we can find a finite affine open cover $X = \bigcup _{i = 1, \ldots , n} X_ i$. Write $X_ i = \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(B_ i)$.
L32: Then $B_ i$ is a finite type $A$-algebra, see Lemma 【15†29.15.2】. Moreover there are finite type $B_ i$-modules $M_ i$ such that $\mathcal{F}|_{X_ i}$ is the quasi-coherent sheaf associated to the $B_ i$-module $M_ i$, see Properties, Lemma 【16†28.17.1】. Next, for each pair of indices $i, j$ choose an ideal $I_{ij} \subset B_ i$ such that $X_ i \setminus X_ i \cap X_ j = V(I_{ij})$ inside $X_ i = \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(B_ i)$. Set $M_{ij} = B_ i/I_{ij}$ and think of it as a $B_ i$-module.
L33: Then $V(I_{ij}) = \text{Supp}(M_{ij})$ and $M_{ij}$ is a finite $B_ i$-module.
L34: At this point we apply Algebra, Lemma 【17†10.118.3】 the pairs $(A \to B_ i, M_{ij})$ and to the pairs $(A \to B_ i, M_ i)$. Thus we obtain nonzero $f_{ij}, f_ i \in A$ such that (a) $A_{f_{ij}} \to B_{i, f_{ij}}$ is flat and of finite presentation and $M_{ij, f_{ij}}$ is flat over $A_{f_{ij}}$ and of finite presentation over $B_{i, f_{ij}}$, and (b) $B_{i, f_ i}$ is flat and of finite presentation over $A_ f$ and $M_{i, f_ i}$ is flat and of finite presentation over $B_{i, f_ i}$.
L35: Set $f = (\prod f_ i) (\prod f_{ij})$. We claim that taking $U = D(f)$ works.
L36: To prove our claim we may replace $A$ by $A_ f$, i.e., perform the base change by $U = \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(A_ f) \to S$. After this base change we see that each of $A \to B_ i$ is flat and of finite presentation and that $M_ i$, $M_{ij}$ are flat over $A$ and of finite presentation over $B_ i$.
L37: This already proves that $X \to S$ is quasi-compact, locally of finite presentation, flat, and that $\mathcal{F}$ is flat over $S$ and of finite presentation over $\mathcal{O}_ X$, see Lemma 【18†29.22.2】 and Properties, Lemma 【19†28.17.2】. Since $M_{ij}$ is of finite presentation over $B_ i$ we see that $X_ i \cap X_ j = X_ i \setminus \text{Supp}(M_{ij})$ is a quasi-compact open of $X_ i$, see Algebra, Lemma 【20†10.40.8】. Hence we see that $X \to S$ is quasi-separated by Schemes, Lemma 【21†26.21.6】.
L38: This proves the proposition. $\square$

L18: 【11†Lemma 37.26.1.】 Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of schemes. Assume $Y$ irreducible with generic point $\eta $ and $f$ of finite type. If $X_\eta $ is nonreduced, then there exists a nonempty open $V \subset Y$ such that for all $y \in V$ the fibre $X_ y$ is nonreduced.
L19: Proof. Let $Y' \subset Y$ be the reduction of $Y$. Let $X' \to Y'$ be the base change of $f$. Note that $Y' \to Y$ induces a bijection on points and that $X' \to X$ identifies fibres. Hence we may assume that $Y'$ is reduced, i.e., integral, see Properties, Lemma 【12†28.3.4】. We may also replace $Y$ by an affine open. Hence we may assume that $Y = \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(A)$ with $A$ a domain. Denote $K$ the fraction field of $A$.
L20: Pick an affine open $\mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(B) = U \subset X$ and a section $h_\eta \in \Gamma (U_\eta , \mathcal{O}_{U_\eta }) = B_ K$ which is nonzero and nilpotent. After shrinking $Y$ we may assume that $h$ comes from $h \in \Gamma (U, \mathcal{O}_ U) = B$. After shrinking $Y$ a bit more we may assume that $h$ is nilpotent. Let $I = \{ b \in B \mid hb = 0\} $ be the annihilator of $h$. Then $C = B/I$ is a finite type $A$-algebra whose generic fiber $(B/I)_ K$ is nonzero (as $h_\eta \not= 0$).
L21: We apply generic flatness to $A \to C$ and $A \to B/hB$, see Algebra, Lemma 【13†10.118.3】, and we obtain a $g \in A$, $g \not= 0$ such that $C_ g$ is free as an $A_ g$-module and $(B/hB)_ g$ is flat as an $A_ g$-module. Replace $Y$ by $D(g) \subset Y$. Now we have the short exact sequence
L22: \[ 0 \to C \to B \to B/hB \to 0. \]
L23: 
L24: with $B/hB$ flat over $A$ and with $C$ nonzero free as an $A$-module. It follows that for any homomorphism $A \to \kappa $ to a field the ring $C \otimes _ A \kappa $ is nonzero and the sequence
L25: 
L26: \[ 0 \to C \otimes _ A \kappa \to B \otimes _ A \kappa \to B/hB \otimes _ A \kappa \to 0 \]
L27: is exact, see Algebra, Lemma 【14†10.39.12】. Note that $B/hB \otimes _ A \kappa = (B \otimes _ A \kappa ) / h(B \otimes _ A \kappa )$ by right exactness of tensor product. Thus we conclude that multiplication by $h$ is not zero on $B \otimes _ A \kappa $. This clearly means that for any point $y \in Y$ the element $h$ restricts to a nonzero element of $U_ y$, whence $X_ y$ is nonreduced. $\square$
L28: 【15†Lemma 37.26.2.】 Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of schemes. Let $g : Y' \to Y$ be any morphism, and denote $f' : X' \to Y'$ the base change of $f$. Then
L29: 
L30: \begin{align*} \{ y' \in Y' \mid X'_{y'}\text{ is geometrically reduced}\} \\ = g^{-1}(\{ y \in Y \mid X_ y\text{ is geometrically reduced}\} ). \end{align*}
L31: Proof. This comes down to the statement that for $y' \in Y'$ with image $y \in Y$ the fibre $X'_{y'} = X_ y \times _ y y'$ is geometrically reduced over $\kappa (y')$ if and only if $X_ y$ is geometrically reduced over $\kappa (y)$. This follows from Varieties, Lemma 【16†33.6.6】. $\square$
L32: 【17†Lemma 37.26.3.】 Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of schemes. Assume $Y$ irreducible with generic point $\eta $ and $f$ of finite type. If $X_\eta $ is not geometrically reduced, then there exists a nonempty open $V \subset Y$ such that for all $y \in V$ the fibre $X_ y$ is not geometrically reduced.
L33: 
L34: Proof. Apply Lemma 【18†37.24.7】 to get
L35: 
L36: \[ \xymatrix{ X' \ar[d]_{f'} \ar[r]_{g'} & X_ V \ar[r] \ar[d] & X \ar[d]^ f \\ Y' \ar[r]^ g & V \ar[r] & Y } \]
L37: with all the properties mentioned in that lemma. Let $\eta '$ be the generic point of $Y'$. Consider the morphism $X' \to X_{Y'}$ (which is the reduction morphism) and the resulting morphism of generic fibres $X'_{\eta '} \to X_{\eta '}$. Since $X'_{\eta '}$ is geometrically reduced, and $X_\eta $ is not this cannot be an isomorphism, see Varieties, Lemma 【16†33.6.6】. Hence $X_{\eta '}$ is nonreduced.
L38: Hence by Lemma 【11†37.26.1】 the fibres of $X_{Y'} \to Y'$ are nonreduced at all points $y' \in V'$ of a nonempty open $V' \subset Y'$. Since $g : Y' \to V$ is a homeomorphism Lemma 【15†37.26.2】 proves that $g(V')$ is the open we are looking for. $\square$
L39: 【19†Lemma 37.26.4.】 Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of schemes. Assume
L40: 
L41:   1. $Y$ is irreducible with generic point $\eta $,
L42: 
L43:   2. $X_\eta $ is geometrically reduced, and
L44: 
L45:   3. $f$ is of finite type.
L46: 
L47: Then there exists a nonempty open subscheme $V \subset Y$ such that $X_ V \to V$ has geometrically reduced fibres.
L48: Proof. Let $Y' \subset Y$ be the reduction of $Y$. Let $X' \to Y'$ be the base change of $f$. Note that $Y' \to Y$ induces a bijection on points and that $X' \to X$ identifies fibres. Hence we may assume that $Y'$ is reduced, i.e., integral, see Properties, Lemma 【12†28.3.4】. We may also replace $Y$ by an affine open. Hence we may assume that $Y = \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(A)$ with $A$ a domain. Denote $K$ the fraction field of $A$.
L49: After shrinking $Y$ a bit we may also assume that $X \to Y$ is flat and of finite presentation, see Morphisms, Proposition 【20†29.28.1】.
L50: As $X_\eta $ is geometrically reduced there exists an open dense subset $V \subset X_\eta $ such that $V \to \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(K)$ is smooth, see Varieties, Lemma 【21†33.25.7】. Let $U \subset X$ be the set of points where $f$ is smooth. By Morphisms, Lemma 【22†29.35.15】 we see that $V \subset U_\eta $. Thus the generic fibre of $U$ is dense in the generic fibre of $X$. Since $X_\eta $ is reduced, it follows that $U_\eta $ is scheme theoretically dense in $X_\eta $, see Morphisms, Lemma 【23†29.7.8】.
L51: We note that as $U \to Y$ is smooth all the fibres of $U \to Y$ are geometrically reduced. Thus it suffices to show that, after shrinking $Y$, for all $y \in Y$ the scheme $U_ y$ is scheme theoretically dense in $X_ y$, see Morphisms, Lemma 【24†29.7.9】. This follows from Lemma 【25†37.24.4】. $\square$
L52: 【26†Lemma 37.26.5.】 Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism which is quasi-compact and locally of finite presentation. Then the set
L53: 
L54: \[ E = \{ y \in Y \mid X_ y\text{ is geometrically reduced}\} \]
L55: 
L56: is locally constructible in $Y$.
L57: Proof. Let $y \in Y$. We have to show that there exists an open neighbourhood $V$ of $y$ in $Y$ such that $E \cap V$ is constructible in $V$. Thus we may assume that $Y$ is affine. Then $X$ is quasi-compact. Choose a finite affine open covering $X = U_1 \cup \ldots \cup U_ n$. Then the fibres of $U_ i \to Y$ at $y$ form an affine open covering of the fibre of $X \to Y$ at $y$. Hence we may assume $X$ is affine as well. Write $Y = \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(A)$.
L58: Write $A = \mathop{\mathrm{colim}}\nolimits A_ i$ as a directed limit of finite type $\mathbf{Z}$-algebras. By Limits, Lemma 【27†32.10.1】 we can find an $i$ and a morphism $f_ i : X_ i \to \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(A_ i)$ of finite presentation whose base change to $Y$ recovers $f$. By Lemma 【15†37.26.2】 it suffices to prove the lemma for $f_ i$. Thus we reduce to the case where $Y$ is the spectrum of a Noetherian ring.
L59: We will use the criterion of Topology, Lemma 【28†5.16.3】 to prove that $E$ is constructible in case $Y$ is a Noetherian scheme. To see this let $Z \subset Y$ be an irreducible closed subscheme with generic point $\xi $. We have to show that $E \cap Z$ either contains a nonempty open subset or is not dense in $Z$. If $X_\xi $ is geometrically reduced, then Lemma 【19†37.26.4】 (applied to the morphism $X_ Z \to Z$) implies that all fibres $X_ y$ are geometrically reduced for a nonempty open $V \subset Z$.
L60: If $X_\xi $ is not geometrically reduced, then Lemma 【17†37.26.3】 (applied to the morphism $X_ Z \to Z$) implies that all fibres $X_ y$ are not geometrically reduced for a nonempty open $V \subset Z$. Thus we win. $\square$
L61: 【29†Lemma 37.26.6.】 Let $f : X \to \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(R)$ be a proper morphism where $R$ is a discrete valuation ring. Assume every irreducible component of $X$ dominates $\mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(R)$ (for example if $f$ is flat) and assume the special fibre is reduced. Then both $X$ and the generic fibre $X_\eta $ are reduced.
L62: Proof. (The fact that a flat morphism satisfies the assumption on irreducible components follows for example from Divisors, Lemma 【30†31.3.1】 or from going down for flat ring maps.) Assume the special fibre $X_ s$ is reduced. Let $x \in X$ be any point, and let us show that $\mathcal{O}_{X, x}$ is reduced; this will prove that $X$ and $X_\eta $ are reduced. Let $x \leadsto x'$ be a specialization with $x'$ in the special fibre; such a specialization exists as a proper morphism is closed.
L63: Consider the local ring $A = \mathcal{O}_{X, x'}$. Then $\mathcal{O}_{X, x}$ is a localization of $A$, so it suffices to show that $A$ is reduced. Let $\pi \in R$ be a uniformizer. If $a \in A$ is nonzero then there exists an $n \geq 0$ and an element $a' \in A$ such that $a = \pi ^ n a'$ and $a' \not\in \pi A$. This follows from Krull intersection theorem (Algebra, Lemma 【31†10.51.4】).
L64: If $a$ is nilpotent the $a$ is contained in all minimal primes of $A$, and hence so is $a'$, because $\pi $ is not contained in any of the minimal primes of $A$ by our assumption on the irreducible components of $X$. Thus $a'$ is nilpotent. But $a'$ maps to a nonzero element of the reduced ring $A/\pi A = \mathcal{O}_{X_ s, x'}$. This is a contradiction unless $A$ is reduced, which is what we wanted to show. $\square$
L65: 【32†Lemma 37.26.7.】 Let $f : X \to Y$ be a flat proper morphism of finite presentation. Then the set $\{ y \in Y \mid X_ y\text{ is geometrically reduced}\} $ is open in $Y$.
L66: Proof. We may assume $Y$ is affine. Then $Y$ is a cofiltered limit of affine schemes of finite type over $\mathbf{Z}$. Hence we can assume $X \to Y$ is the base change of $X_0 \to Y_0$ where $Y_0$ is the spectrum of a finite type $\mathbf{Z}$-algebra and $X_0 \to Y_0$ is flat and proper. See Limits, Lemma 【27†32.10.1】, 【33†32.8.7】, and 【34†32.13.1】.
L67: Since the formation of the set of points where the fibres are geometrically reduced commutes with base change (Lemma 【15†37.26.2】), we may assume the base is Noetherian.
L68: Assume $Y$ is Noetherian. The set is constructible by Lemma 【26†37.26.5】. Hence it suffices to show the set is stable under generalization (Topology, Lemma 【35†5.19.10】). By Properties, Lemma 【36†28.5.10】 we reduce to the case where $Y = \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(R)$, $R$ is a discrete valuation ring, and the closed fibre $X_ y$ is geometrically reduced. To show: the generic fibre $X_\eta $ is geometrically reduced.
L69: If not then there exists a finite extension $L$ of the fraction field of $R$ such that $X_ L$ is not reduced, see Varieties, Lemma 【37†33.6.4】. There exists a discrete valuation ring $R' \subset L$ with fraction field $L$ dominating $R$, see Algebra, Lemma 【38†10.120.18】. After replacing $R$ by $R'$ we reduce to Lemma 【29†37.26.6】. $\square$

L16: ## 37.27 Irreducible components of fibres
L17: 
L18: 【11†Lemma 37.27.1.】 Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of schemes. Assume $Y$ irreducible with generic point $\eta $ and $f$ of finite type. If $X_\eta $ has $n$ irreducible components, then there exists a nonempty open $V \subset Y$ such that for all $y \in V$ the fibre $X_ y$ has at least $n$ irreducible components.
L19: Proof. As the question is purely topological we may replace $X$ and $Y$ by their reductions. In particular this implies that $Y$ is integral, see Properties, Lemma 【12†28.3.4】. Let $X_\eta = X_{1, \eta } \cup \ldots \cup X_{n, \eta }$ be the decomposition of $X_\eta $ into irreducible components. Let $X_ i \subset X$ be the reduced closed subscheme whose generic fibre is $X_{i, \eta }$.
L20: Note that $Z_{i, j} = X_ i \cap X_ j$ is a closed subset of $X_ i$ whose generic fibre $Z_{i, j, \eta }$ is nowhere dense in $X_{i, \eta }$. Hence after shrinking $Y$ we may assume that $Z_{i, j, y}$ is nowhere dense in $X_{i, y}$ for every $y \in Y$, see Lemma 【13†37.24.3】. After shrinking $Y$ some more we may assume that $X_ y = \bigcup X_{i, y}$ for $y \in Y$, see Lemma 【14†37.24.5】.
L21: Moreover, after shrinking $Y$ we may assume that each $X_ i \to Y$ is flat and of finite presentation, see Morphisms, Proposition 【15†29.28.1】. The morphisms $X_ i \to Y$ are open, see Morphisms, Lemma 【16†29.26.10】. Thus there exists an open neighbourhood $V$ of $\eta $ which is contained in $f(X_ i)$ for each $i$.
L22: For each $y \in V$ the schemes $X_{i, y}$ are nonempty closed subsets of $X_ y$, we have $X_ y = \bigcup X_{i, y}$ and the intersections $Z_{i, j, y} = X_{i, y} \cap X_{j, y}$ are not dense in $X_{i, y}$. Clearly this implies that $X_ y$ has at least $n$ irreducible components. $\square$
L23: 【17†Lemma 37.27.2.】 Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of schemes. Let $g : Y' \to Y$ be any morphism, and denote $f' : X' \to Y'$ the base change of $f$. Then
L24: 
L25: \begin{align*} \{ y' \in Y' \mid X'_{y'}\text{ is geometrically irreducible}\} \\ = g^{-1}(\{ y \in Y \mid X_ y\text{ is geometrically irreducible}\} ). \end{align*}
L26: Proof. This comes down to the statement that for $y' \in Y'$ with image $y \in Y$ the fibre $X'_{y'} = X_ y \times _ y y'$ is geometrically irreducible over $\kappa (y')$ if and only if $X_ y$ is geometrically irreducible over $\kappa (y)$. This follows from Varieties, Lemma 【18†33.8.2】. $\square$
L27: 
L28: 【19†Lemma 37.27.3.】 Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of schemes. Let
L29: 
L30: \[ n_{X/Y} : Y \to \{ 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots , \infty \} \]
L31: be the function which associates to $y \in Y$ the number of irreducible components of $(X_ y)_ K$ where $K$ is a separably closed extension of $\kappa (y)$. This is well defined and if $g : Y' \to Y$ is a morphism then
L32: 
L33: \[ n_{X'/Y'} = n_{X/Y} \circ g \]
L34: 
L35: where $X' \to Y'$ is the base change of $f$.
L36: 
L37: Proof. Suppose that $y' \in Y'$ has image $y \in Y$. Suppose $K \supset \kappa (y)$ and $K' \supset \kappa (y')$ are separably closed extensions. Then we may choose a commutative diagram
L38: \[ \xymatrix{ K \ar[r] & K'' & K' \ar[l] \\ \kappa (y) \ar[u] \ar[rr] & & \kappa (y') \ar[u] } \]
L39: 
L40: of fields. The result follows as the morphisms of schemes
L41: 
L42: \[ \xymatrix{ (X'_{y'})_{K'} & (X'_{y'})_{K''} = (X_ y)_{K''} \ar[l] \ar[r] & (X_ y)_ K } \]
L43: 
L44: induce bijections between irreducible components, see Varieties, Lemma 【20†33.8.8】. $\square$
L45: 【21†Lemma 37.27.4.】 Let $A$ be a domain with fraction field $K$. Let $P \in A[x_1, \ldots , x_ n]$. Denote $\overline{K}$ the algebraic closure of $K$. Assume $P$ is irreducible in $\overline{K}[x_1, \ldots , x_ n]$. Then there exists a $f \in A$ such that $P^\varphi \in \kappa [x_1, \ldots , x_ n]$ is irreducible for all homomorphisms $\varphi : A_ f \to \kappa $ into fields.
L46: Proof. There exists an automorphism $\Psi $ of $A[x_1, \ldots , x_ n]$ over $A$ such that $\Psi (P) = ax_ n^ d +$ lower order terms in $x_ n$ with $a \not= 0$, see Algebra, Lemma 【22†10.115.2】. We may replace $P$ by $\Psi (P)$ and we may replace $A$ by $A_ a$. Thus we may assume that $P$ is monic in $x_ n$ of degree $d > 0$. For $i = 1, \ldots , n - 1$ let $d_ i$ be the degree of $P$ in $x_ i$.
L47: Note that this implies that $P^\varphi $ is monic of degree $d$ in $x_ n$ and has degree $\leq d_ i$ in $x_ i$ for every homomorphism $\varphi : A \to \kappa $ where $\kappa $ is a field. Thus if $P^\varphi $ is reducible, then we can write
L48: \[ P^\varphi = Q_1 Q_2 \]
L49: 
L50: with $Q_1, Q_2$ monic of degree $e_1, e_2 \geq 0$ in $x_ n$ with $e_1 + e_2 = d$ and having degree $\leq d_ i$ in $x_ i$ for $i = 1, \ldots , n - 1$. In other words we can write
L51: 
L52: 【23†37.27.4.1】
L53: 
L54: \begin{equation} \label{more-morphisms-equation-factors} Q_ j = x_ n^{e_ j} + \sum \nolimits _{0 \leq l < e_ j} \left( \sum \nolimits _{L \in \mathcal{L}} a_{j, l, L} x^ L \right) x_ n^ l \end{equation}
L55: where the sum is over the set $\mathcal{L}$ of multi-indices $L$ of the form $L = (l_1, \ldots , l_{n - 1})$ with $0 \leq l_ i \leq d_ i$. For any $e_1, e_2 \geq 0$ with $e_1 + e_2 = d$ we consider the $A$-algebra
L56: 
L57: \[ B_{e_1, e_2} = A[\{ a_{1, l, L}\} _{0 \leq l < e_1, L \in \mathcal{L}}, \{ a_{2, l, L}\} _{0 \leq l < e_2, L \in \mathcal{L}}]/(\text{relations}) \]
L58: 
L59: where the $(\text{relations})$ is the ideal generated by the coefficients of the polynomial
L60: \[ P - Q_1Q_2 \in A[\{ a_{1, l, L}\} _{0 \leq l < e_1, L \in \mathcal{L}}, \{ a_{2, l, L}\} _{0 \leq l < e_2, L \in \mathcal{L}}][x_1, \ldots , x_ n] \]
L61: with $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ defined as in (【23†37.27.4.1】). OK, and the assumption that $P$ is irreducible over $\overline{K}$ implies that there does not exist any $A$-algebra homomorphism $B_{e_1, e_2} \to \overline{K}$. By the Hilbert Nullstellensatz, see Algebra, Theorem 【24†10.34.1】 this means that $B_{e_1, e_2} \otimes _ A K = 0$. As $B_{e_1, e_2}$ is a finitely generated $A$-algebra this signifies that we can find an $f_{e_1, e_2} \in A$ such that $(B_{e_1, e_2})_{f_{e_1, e_2}} = 0$.
L62: By construction this means that if $\varphi : A_{f_{e_1, e_2}} \to \kappa $ is a homomorphism to a field, then $P^\varphi $ does not have a factorization $P^\varphi = Q_1 Q_2$ with $Q_1$ of degree $e_1$ in $x_ n$ and $Q_2$ of degree $e_2$ in $x_ n$. Thus taking $f = \prod _{e_1, e_2 \geq 0, e_1 + e_2 = d} f_{e_1, e_2}$ we win. $\square$
L63: 【25†Lemma 37.27.5.】 Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of schemes. Assume
L64: 
L65:   1. $Y$ is irreducible with generic point $\eta $,
L66: 
L67:   2. $X_\eta $ is geometrically irreducible, and
L68: 
L69:   3. $f$ is of finite type.
L70: 
L71: Then there exists a nonempty open subscheme $V \subset Y$ such that $X_ V \to V$ has geometrically irreducible fibres.
L72: 
L73: First proof of Lemma 【25†37.27.5】. We give two proofs of the lemma. These are essentially equivalent; the second is more self contained but a bit longer. Choose a diagram
L74: \[ \xymatrix{ X' \ar[d]_{f'} \ar[r]_{g'} & X_ V \ar[r] \ar[d] & X \ar[d]^ f \\ Y' \ar[r]^ g & V \ar[r] & Y } \]
L75: as in Lemma 【26†37.24.7】. Note that the generic fibre of $f'$ is the reduction of the generic fibre of $f$ (see Lemma 【27†37.24.6】) and hence is geometrically irreducible. Suppose that the lemma holds for the morphism $f'$. Then after shrinking $V$ all the fibres of $f'$ are geometrically irreducible. As $X' = (Y' \times _ V X_ V)_{red}$ this implies that all the fibres of $Y' \times _ V X_ V$ are geometrically irreducible.
L76: Hence by Lemma 【17†37.27.2】 all the fibres of $X_ V \to V$ are geometrically irreducible and we win. In this way we see that we may assume that the generic fibre is geometrically reduced as well as geometrically irreducible and we may assume $Y = \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(A)$ with $A$ a domain.
L77: Let $x \in X_\eta $ be the generic point. As $X_\eta $ is geometrically irreducible and reduced we see that $L = \kappa (x)$ is a finitely generated extension of $K = \kappa (\eta )$ which is geometrically reduced and geometrically irreducible, see Varieties, Lemmas 【28†33.6.2】 and 【29†33.8.6】. In particular the field extension $L/K$ is separable, see Algebra, Lemma 【30†10.44.2】.
L78: Hence we can find $x_1, \ldots , x_{r + 1} \in L$ which generate $L$ over $K$ and such that $x_1, \ldots , x_ r$ is a transcendence basis for $L$ over $K$, see Algebra, Lemma 【31†10.42.3】. Let $P \in K(x_1, \ldots , x_ r)[T]$ be the minimal polynomial for $x_{r + 1}$. Clearing denominators we may assume that $P$ has coefficients in $A[x_1, \ldots , x_ r]$.
L79: Note that as $L$ is geometrically reduced and geometrically irreducible over $K$, the polynomial $P$ is irreducible in $\overline{K}[x_1, \ldots , x_ r, T]$ where $\overline{K}$ is the algebraic closure of $K$. Denote
L80: \[ B' = A[x_1, \ldots , x_{r + 1}]/(P(x_{r + 1})) \]
L81: 
L82: and set $X' = \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(B')$. By construction the fraction field of $B'$ is isomorphic to $L = \kappa (x)$ as $K$-extensions. Hence there exists an open $U \subset X$, and open $U' \subset X'$ and a $Y$-isomorphism $U \to U'$, see Morphisms, Lemma 【32†29.51.7】. Here is a diagram:
L83: 
L84: \[ \xymatrix{ X \ar[rd] & U \ar[l] \ar@{=}[r] \ar[d] & U' \ar[r] \ar[d] & X' \ar[ld] \ar@{=}[r] & \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(B') \\ & Y \ar@{=}[r] & Y & } \]

A model L of L defines a continuous metric φL on L, as follows. Cover X with finitely
many open subschemes Ui with a trivializing section τi of L. Since X is in particular proper
over K ◦ , X an = X i is covered by the compact sets Uii . We may thus define a continuous
metric φL on Lan by requiring that |τi |φL = 1 on Uii . This is indeed well-defined, since any
other trivializing section of L on Ui is of the form ui τi with ui ∈ O× (Ui ) a unit, and hence
|ui | ≡ 1 on Uii .
Example 5.9. If K is trivially valued, the model metric defined by the unique model (X, L)
is called the trivial metric of L.
Lemma 5.10. Let L be a model of L, with corresponding metric φL .
      (i) For each m ∈ Z we have φmL = mφL .
     (ii) If a model X ′ dominates X , then the pull-back L′ of L to X ′ satisfies φL′ = φL .
Proof. If τ is trivializing section of L on an open set U , then τ m is a trivializing section
of mL, and the pull-back of τ is a local trivialization of L′ on the inverse image U ′ , which
satisfies U ′i = U i since U ′ is proper over U (cf. Lemma 4.6).                             

  If L is now a Q-line bundle on X, a Q-model of L is defined as a Q-line bundle L on a
projective model X of X such that mL is a model of mL for some m ≥ 1. By Lemma 5.10 (i),
the metric φL := m−1 φmL on L is independent of the choice of m.
Definition 5.11. A model metric on a Q-line bundle L is a metric of the form φ = φL ,
where L is a Q-model of L. A model function is a model metric φ on OX , identified with
the continuous function − log |1|φ on X an .
  A model function f is thus determined by a vertical Q-Cartier divisor D on some projective
model X of X. Every line bundle L on X admits a model metric φ, and any other model
metric on L is then of the form φ + f with f a model function.
                 NORMS, DETERMINANT OF COHOMOLOGY AND FEKETE POINTS                            41

Theorem 5.12. Assume that K is either discretely (or trivially) valued, or algebraically
closed. Let L, L′ be two models of a the same line bundle L, determined on models X , X ′ of
X. Then the model metrics φL , φL′ on L coincide iff the pullbacks of L, L′ to some model
X ′′ dominating both X and X ’ are equal.
Proof. If the pullbacks of L, L′ to some high enough model agree, then φL = φL′ , by
Lemma 5.10. Assume conversely that φL = φL′ . By Theorem 4.20, X and X ′ are dom-
inated by a model X ′′ which is integrally closed in X. After pulling back L and L′ to X ′′ ,
we may thus assume that L and L′ are determined on X integrally closed in X, and we
then claim that L = L′ . To see thus, let U = Spec(A) be an affine open subscheme of X
with trivializing sections τ ∈ H0 (U , L), τ ′ ∈ H0 (U , L′ ). Since L, L′ are both models of the
same line bundle L, the restrictions of τ, τ ′ to the generic fiber U = Spec(AK ) of U satisfy
τ ′ |U = uτ |U with u ∈ AK a unit. As φL and φL′ coincide, the definition of model metrics
yields |u| ≡ 1 on U i . By Theorem 4.19, A coincides with the unit ball of k · ksup on AK . As
kuksup = ku−1 ksup = 1, it follows that u and u−1 belong to A, i.e. u is a unit in A, and we
conclude that L = L′ .                                                                         
  The next result describes the behavior of model metrics under pullback.
Proposition 5.13. Let L be a Q-line bundle on X, and φL be the model metric determined
by a Q-model L of L on a model X of X. For any projective morphism f : Y → X, the
induced metric f ⋆ φ on f ⋆ L is also a model metric. More precisely, the family of projective
models Y of Y such that f extends to a K ◦ -morphism f : Y → X is cofinal in all projective
models, and we have f ⋆ φL = φf ⋆ L for any such model Y.
   If f : Y → X is flat, then Y can further be assumed to be flat over X .
Proof. Pick a projective model Y ′ of Y , and denote by Y the schematic (or flat) closure in
Y ′ ×K ◦ X of the graph of f . Then Y dominates Y ′ , and the projection Y → X extends f .
To see the last point, we may assume that L is a line bundle. Let (Ui ) be a finite open cover
of Y with trivializing sections τi ∈ H0 (Ui , L). Then (f −1 (Ui )) is an open cover of Y with
trivializing sections f ⋆ τi for f ⋆ L, and the result easily follows.
For the last point, by the Raynaud–Gruson flattening theorem [RG71], we can blow up X
and take the proper transform of Y to obtain a flat morphism f : Y ′ → X ′ of models. By
Lemma 5.10 this does not change the metrics induced by the models.                          
  We are now in a position to compare model metrics and Fubini–Study metrics (see [CMor18,
Proposition 3.8] for a related result).
Theorem 5.14. For a continuous metric φ on a Q-line bundle L over X, the following are
equivalent:
     (i) φ is a pure Fubini–Study metric;
    (ii) φ is a model metric determined by a semiample Q-model L of L, i.e. mL is a globally
         generated line bundle when m ∈ N is sufficiently divisible.

L0@P0: arXiv:1404.0279v1 [math.AG] 1 Apr 2014
L1@P0: ON THE STRUCTURE OF NONARCHIMEDEAN ANALYTIC CURVES
L2@P0: MATTHEW BAKER, SAM PAYNE, AND JOSEPH RABINOFF
L3@P0: ABSTRACT. Let K be an algebraically closed, complete nonarchimedean field and let X be a smooth
L4@P0: K-curve. In this paper we elaborate on several aspects of the structure of the Berkovich analytic space
L5@P0: Xan. We define semistable vertex sets of Xan and their associated skeleta, which are essentially finite
L6@P0: metric graphs embedded in Xan. We prove a folklore theorem which states that semistable vertex sets
L7@P0: of X are in natural bijective correspondence with semistable models of X, thus showing that our notion
L8@P0: of skeleton coincides with the standard definition of Berkovich [Ber90]. We use the skeletal theory to
L9@P0: define a canonical metric on H(Xan) ≔ Xan r X(K), and we give a proof of Thuillier’s nonarchimedean
L10@P0: Poincaré-Lelong formula in this language using results of Bosch and Lütkebohmert.
L11@P0: 1. INTRODUCTION
L12@P0: Throughout this paper we let K denote an algebraically closed field which is complete with respect
L13@P0: to a nontrivial, nonarchimedean valuation val : K → R ∪ {∞}. Let R be the valuation ring of K, mR
L14@P0: its maximal ideal, and k its residue field. In this situation, R is not Noetherian and k is algebraically
L15@P0: closed. We let | · | = exp(− val(·)) be an associated absolute value and let G = val(K×) ⊂ R be the
L16@P0: value group.
L17@P0: 1.1. Let X be a smooth, proper, connected algebraic K-curve and let Xan be its analytification in the
L18@P0: sense of Berkovich [Ber90]. The purpose of this note is to elaborate on the following aspects of the
L19@P0: structure of Xan:
L20@P0: (1) We define semistable vertex sets of X and their associated skeleta, which are finite metric
L21@P0: graphs contained in Xan.
L22@P0: (2) We make explicit the bijective correspondence between the semistable vertex sets of X and
L23@P0: the semistable models of X.
L24@P0: (3) We show that ‘most’ of X can be covered by skeleta as above, and use this fact to define a
L25@P0: canonical metric on H(Xan) ≔ Xan r X(K) such that the resulting metric space is locally
L26@P0: modeled on an R-tree.
L27@P0: (4) We use results of Bosch and Lütkebohmert to prove Thuillier’s nonarchimedean analogue of
L28@P0: the Poincaré-Lelong formula. This includes the fact that the valuation of a nonzero rational
L29@P0: function on X is a piecewise affine function on H(Xan), which is moreover harmonic in the
L30@P0: sense that the sum of the outgoing slopes at any point is zero.
L31@P0: The above results, while very useful and in large part well-known to experts, are often difficult or
L32@P0: impossible to extract from the literature, although Ducros [Duc13] is preparing a book on the subject.
L33@P0: In [BPR11] we apply these ideas to study the relationship between the analytification of a curve X
L34@P0: and its tropicalization with respect to a rational map to a torus. In particular, we study the metric
L35@P0: aspects of the tropicalization map and the relationship between skeleta and tropicalizations of X.
L36@P0: 1.2. Skeleta and semistable models. The theory of skeleta goes back to Berkovich [Ber90, Ber99],
L37@P0: and is elaborated somewhat in the case of curves in Thuillier’s (unpublished) thesis [Thu05]. In
L38@P0: Berkovich’s approach, a skeleton is a subset of Xan which is associated to a semistable model of X.
L39@P0: In contrast, we define the skeleton in terms of a semistable vertex set of X (called a triangulation
L40@P0: in [Duc08]; see also Temkin’s lecture notes [Tem]), which is a finite set V of type-2 points of Xan such
L41@P0: that Xan r V is a disjoint union of open balls and finitely many open annuli. This approach has the
L42@P0: advantage that it only makes reference to the analytic space Xan and is not conceptually tied to the
L43@P0: semistable reduction theory of X, thus making certain constructions more natural.
L44@P0-1: 12 MATTHEW BAKER, SAM PAYNE, AND JOSEPH RABINOFF

L84@P1: bijective, thus unifying the two notions of skeleta. See Theorem 4.11 and Proposition 4.10.
L85@P1: Theorem. The association X 7→ VX is a bijective correspondence from the set of semistable models of X
L86@P1: to the set of semistable vertex sets of X. Moreover, there exists a morphism of semistable models X → X′

L88@P1: 1.4. In §5 we turn our attention to the metric nature of the analytic curve Xan. This is worked
L89@P1: out ‘by hand’ in the case X = P1 by Baker and Rumely [BR10], but does not otherwise explicitly
L90@P1: appear in the literature. We will prove that the metric graph structures on each skeleton of Xan are
L91@P1: compatible, and that the resulting metric on their union extends by continuity to a unique metric on
L92@P1: H(Xan) = Xan r X(K). The resulting metric space is locally modeled on an R-tree. At this point it
L93@P1: is straightforward to give a proof of Thuillier’s Poincaré-Lelong formula [Thu05, Proposition 3.3.15]
L94@P1: using classical machinery of Bosch and Lütkebohmert. We will do so without developing the harmonic
L95@P1: analysis necessary to give the statement of Thuillier’s theorem in terms of the nonarchimedean ddc
L96@P1: operator; for this reason we call the theorem the Slope Formula.
L97@P1: In the statement of the Slope Formula, we say that a function F : H(Xan) → R is piecewise affine
L98@P1: with integer slopes provided that, for every isometric embedding α : [a, b] ֒→ H(Xan), the composition
L99@P1-2: F ◦α is a piecewise affine function with integer slopes on the interval [a, b]. We define the set of tangentON THE STRUCTURE OF NONARCHIMEDEAN ANALYTIC CURVES 3

In Section 4, we show the coincidence of the notions of subharmonic and psh for
continuous functions on the analytification of algebraic curves. We start by showing in
Proposition 4.3 that a lisse subharmonic function is psh. Since the psh functions form a
sheaf (see Proposition 3.19), it remains to show the assertion for an open neighborhood
of every point. The complicated case is a point of type II. The strategy is to find an open
neighborhood such that the lisse function f can be written as an R-linear combination
of model functions. One can deduce that the Monge-Ampère measure of the restriction
of f coincides with the measure ddc f defined by Thuillier since it does for every model
function, and the claim follows.
   Due to the analogue of Thuillier’s monotone regularization theorem (see Proposition
2.8), we get the following theorem.
Theorem 1. Let W be an open subset of X an and f : W → [−∞, ∞) be a subharmonic
function, then f is psh.
   We continue in Section 4 by proving the other implication for continuous functions,
i.e. the following theorem.
Theorem 2. Let W be an open subset of X an and f : W → R be a continuous function.
If f is psh, then f is subharmonic.
   To obtain this result, we first show in Lemma 4.6 that for every non-subharmonic
function f ,Rthere has to beRa specific non-negative model function g with compact support
such that f MA(g) = f ddc g < 0. The proof of the theorem is by contradiction,
and we assume that such a function g exists. RWe approximate g by non-negative
                                                                       R            smooth
functions gk with compact support such that f dMA(g) = limk→∞ f ∧d′ d′′ gk . Since f
is psh, the left hand side of the equation is non-negative, and so f has to be subharmonic.
The idea of the construction of these functions gk is based on [CD12, Proposition 6.3.2]
and we explain the modification in several steps.
   In Section 5, we give some applications of this coincidence of the two notions of
subharmonicity for continuous functions. Since we know that subharmonicity in the
sense of Thuillier is stable under pullback (see Proposition 2.6), we can deduce the
following corollary from the theorems above.
Corollary 3. Let X, X ′ be smooth proper algebraic curves over K and ϕ : W ′ → W
be a morphism of K-analytic spaces for open subsets W ⊂ X an and W ′ ⊂ (X ′ )an . If a
continuous function f : W → R is psh on W , then ϕ∗ f is psh on ϕ−1 (W ).
  Furthermore, if X satisfies some certain properties, e.g. X is the projective line
or a Mumford curve, we obtain a monotone regularization theorem in the setting of
Chambert-Loir and Ducros using the one in Thuillier’s setting (see Proposition 2.8). Note
that we need all harmonic functions on X an to be smooth in the sense of Chambert-Loir
and Ducros to prove the statement.
Corollary 4. Let X be a smooth proper curve over K. If the residue field K  e is algebraic
over a finite field or X is the projective line or a Mumford curve, then every continuous
psh function f : W → R on an open subset W of X an is locally psh-approximable. More

L24: 【8†Lemma 37.53.6.】 Let $f : X \to S$ be a morphism of schemes. Assume
L25:   1. $f$ is proper,
L26: 
L27:   2. $S$ is integral with generic point $\xi $,
L28: 
L29:   3. $S$ is normal,
L30: 
L31:   4. $X$ is reduced,
L32: 
L33:   5. every generic point of an irreducible component of $X$ maps to $\xi $,
L34: 
L35:   6. we have $H^0(X_\xi , \mathcal{O}) = \kappa (\xi )$.
L36: 
L37: Then $f_*\mathcal{O}_ X = \mathcal{O}_ S$ and $f$ has geometrically connected fibres.
L38: Proof. Apply Theorem 【10†37.53.5】 to get a factorization $X \to S' \to S$. It is enough to show that $S' = S$. This will follow from Morphisms, Lemma 【15†29.55.8】. Namely, $S'$ is reduced because $X$ is reduced (Morphisms, Lemma 【16†29.54.8】). The morphism $S' \to S$ is integral by the theorem cited above. Every generic point of $S'$ lies over $\xi $ by Morphisms, Lemma 【17†29.54.9】 and assumption (5).
L39: On the other hand, since $S'$ is the relative spectrum of $f_*\mathcal{O}_ X$ we see that the scheme theoretic fibre $S'_\xi $ is the spectrum of $H^0(X_\xi , \mathcal{O})$ which is equal to $\kappa (\xi )$ by assumption. Hence $S'$ is an integral scheme with function field equal to the function field of $S$. This finishes the proof. $\square$

L22: 【8†Lemma 29.55.12.】 Let $X$ be an irreducible, geometrically unibranch scheme. The normalization morphism $\nu : X^\nu \to X$ is a universal homeomorphism.
L23: Proof. We have to show that $\nu $ is integral, universally injective, and surjective, see Lemma 【14†29.46.5】. By Lemma 【15†29.55.5】 the morphism $\nu $ is integral. Let $x \in X$ and set $A = \mathcal{O}_{X, x}$. Since $X$ is irreducible we see that $A$ has a single minimal prime $\mathfrak p$ and $A_{red} = A/\mathfrak p$. By Lemma 【16†29.55.4】 the stalk $A' = (\nu _*\mathcal{O}_{X^\nu })_ x$ is the integral closure of $A$ in the fraction field of $A_{red}$.
L24: By More on Algebra, Definition 【17†15.108.1】 we see that $A'$ has a single prime $\mathfrak m'$ lying over $\mathfrak m_ x \subset A$ and $\kappa (\mathfrak m')/\kappa (x)$ is purely inseparable. Hence $\nu $ is bijective (hence surjective) and universally injective by Lemma 【18†29.10.2】. $\square$

L32: Proof. (We observe that $X$ is separated and finite type as a locally closed subscheme of a projective space.) Let us use the notation introduced above the statement of the lemma. We consider the projections
L33: \[ \xymatrix{ \mathbf{A}^ r_ k \times _ k X \ar[d] & H_{univ} \ar[l] \ar[ld]^ p \ar[r] \ar[rd]_ q & \mathbf{A}^ r_ k \times _ k X \ar[d] \\ X & & \mathbf{A}^ r_ k } \]
L34: Let $\Sigma \subset H_{univ}$ be the singular locus of the morphsm $q : H_{univ} \to \mathbf{A}^ r_ k$, i.e., the set of points where $q$ is not smooth. Then $\Sigma $ is closed because the smooth locus of a morphism is open by definition. Since the fibre of a smooth morphism is smooth, it suffices to prove $q(\Sigma )$ is contained in a proper closed subset of $\mathbf{A}^ r_ k$.
L35: Since $\Sigma $ (with reduced induced scheme structure) is a finite type scheme over $k$ it suffices to prove $\dim (\Sigma ) < r$ This follows from Lemma 【14†33.20.4】. Since dimensions aren't changed by replacing $k$ by a bigger field (Morphisms, Lemma 【15†29.29.3】), we may and do assume $k$ is algebraically closed.
L36: By dimension theory (Lemma 【14†33.20.4】), it suffices to prove that for $x \in X \setminus Z$ closed we have $p^{-1}(\{ x\} ) \cap \Sigma $ has dimension $< r - \dim (X')$ where $X'$ is the unique irreducible component of $X$ containing $x$. As $X$ is smooth over $k$ and $x$ is a closed point we have $\dim (X') = \dim \mathfrak m_ x/\mathfrak m_ x^2$ (Morphisms, Lemma 【16†29.35.12】 and Algebra, Lemma 【17†10.140.1】). Thus we win if

(For example, if $x' \in X'$ is a closed point, then we can take the open corresponding to those vectors $v \in V$ such that $\psi (v)$ does not vanish at $x'$.

Then the fibres of $q^{-1}(U) \to U$ are effective Cartier divisors on the fibres of $U \times _ k X \to U$ (because a nonvanishing section of an invertible module on an integral scheme is a regular section). Hence the morphism $q^{-1}(U) \to U$ is flat by Divisors, Lemma 【18†31.19.9】.

L22: 【8†Lemma 33.48.3.】 Let $k$ be a field. Let $X$ be a proper scheme over $k$. Let $\mathcal{L}$ be an ample invertible $\mathcal{O}_ X$-module. Let $s \in \Gamma (X, \mathcal{L})$. Assume
L23: 
L24:   1. $s$ is a regular section (Divisors, Definition 【14†31.15.6】),
L25: 
L26:   2. for every closed point $x \in X$ we have $\text{depth}(\mathcal{O}_{X, x}) \geq 2$, and
L27: 
L28:   3. $X$ is connected.
L29: 
L30: Then the zero scheme $Z(s)$ of $s$ is connected.
L31: Proof. Since $s$ is a regular section, so is $s^ n \in \Gamma (X, \mathcal{L}^{\otimes n})$ for all $n > 1$. Moreover, the inclusion morphism $Z(s) \to Z(s^ n)$ is a bijection on underlying topological spaces. Hence if $Z(s)$ is disconnected, so is $Z(s^ n)$. Now consider the canonical short exact sequence
L32: 
L33: \[ 0 \to \mathcal{L}^{\otimes -n} \xrightarrow {s^ n} \mathcal{O}_ X \to \mathcal{O}_{Z(s^ n)} \to 0 \]
L34: Consider the $k$-algebra $R_ n = \Gamma (X, \mathcal{O}_{Z(s^ n)})$. If $Z(s)$ is disconnected, i.e., $Z(s^ n)$ is disconnected, then either $R_ n$ is zero in case $Z(s^ n) = \emptyset $ or $R_ n$ contains a nontrivial idempotent in case $Z(s^ n) = U \amalg V$ with $U, V \subset Z(s^ n)$ open and nonempty (the reader may wish to consult Lemma 【15†33.9.3】). Thus the map $\Gamma (X, \mathcal{O}_ X) \to R_ n$ cannot be an isomorphism.
L35: It follows that either $H^0(X, \mathcal{L}^{\otimes -n})$ or $H^1(X, \mathcal{L}^{\otimes -n})$ is nonzero for infinitely many positive $n$. This contradicts Lemma 【16†33.48.1】 or 【10†33.48.2】 and the proof is complete. $\square$

L16: > Abstract: This article contains an elementary constructive proof of resolution of singularities in characteristic zero. Our proof applies in particular to schemes of finite type and to analytic spaces (so we recover the great theorems of Hironaka). We introduce a discrete local invariant $\inv_X (a)$ whose maximum locus determines a smooth centre of blowing up, leading to desingularization.
L17: To define $\inv_X$, we need only to work with a category of local-ringed spaces $X=(|X|,{\cal O}_X)$ satisfying certain natural conditions. If $a\in |X|$, then $\inv_X(a)$ depends only on $\widehat{\cal O}_{X,a}$. More generally, $\inv_X(a)$ is defined inductively after any sequence of blowings-up whose centres have only normal crossings with respect to the exceptional divisors and lie in the constant loci of $\inv_X(\cdot)$. The paper is self-contained and includes detailed examples.
L18: One of our goals is that the reader understand the desingularization theorem, rather than simply ``know'' it is true.
L19: Comments:  | PS, Only the first chapter is available from Algebraic- Geometry E-prints. A complete manuscript (86 pages, approx. 340K) is available on WWW as a gzipped DVI file in binary mode at this ftp URL A hard copy is also available on request

L0@P0: INTRODUCTION TO BERKOVICH ANALYTIC SPACES
L1@P0: MICHAEL TEMKIN
L2@P0: 1. Introduction
L3@P0: This paper is a preliminary version of the lecture notes that accompanies my
L4@P0: introductory course on Berkovich analytic spaces at Summer School ”Berkovich
L5@P0: spaces” at Institut de Mathmatiques de Jussieu, 29 June – 9 July, 2010.
L6@P0: 1.1. Berkovich spaces and some history.
L7@P0: 1.1.1. Naive non-archimedean analytic spaces. Since non-archimedean complete real
L8@P0: valued fields (e.g. Qp) were discovered in the beginning of the century, it was very
L9@P0: natural to try to develop a theory of analytic spaces over such a field k analogously
L10@P0: to the theory of complex analytic spaces. At least, one can naturally define analytic
L11@P0: functions on a subset V of the naive affine line A1
L12@P0: k = k as the convergent power
L13@P0: series on V . This allowed to introduce some naive k-analytic spaces, but the theory
L14@P0: was not reach enough. Actually, a global theory of such varieties does not make too
L15@P0: much sense because the topology of k is totaly disconnected. In particular, locally
L16@P0: analytic (and even constant) functions do not have to be globally analytic.
L17@P0: 1.1.2. Rigid geometry. In his study of elliptic curves with bad reduction over k,
L18@P0: Tate discovered in 1960ies that these curves admit a natural uniformization by
L19@P0: Gm. The latter was given as an abstract isomorphism of groups k
L20@P0: ×/qZf→E(k), and
L21@P0: even such expert as Grothendieck doubted at first that this is not an accidental
L22@P0: brute force isomorphism. Tate suspected, however, that his isomorphism can be
L23@P0: interpreted as an analytic one, and he had to develop a good global theory of
L24@P0: non-archimedean analytic spaces to make this rigorous. This research resulted in
L25@P0: Tate’s definition of rigid geometry, whose starting idea was to simply forbid all bad
L26@P0: open coverings (responsible for disconnectedness) and to shrink the set of analytic
L27@P0: functions accordingly. As a result, one obtains a good theory of sheaves of analytic
L28@P0: functions, but the underlying topological spaces have to be replaced with certain
L29@P0: topologized (or Grothendieck) categories, also called G-topological spaces.
L30@P0: 1.1.3. Berkovich spaces. More recently, few other approaches to ”right” non-archimedean geometry were discovered: Raynaud’s theory of formal models, Berkovich’
L31@P0: analytic geometry and Huber’s adic geometry. They all allow to define (nearly)
L32@P0: the same categories of k-analytic spaces, but provide the analogs of rigid spaces
L33@P0: with additional structures invisible in the classical Tate’s theory. Also, they extend
L34@P0: the category of rigid spaces in different directions. Here we only discuss Berkovich’
L35@P0: theory, which was developed in [Ber1] and [Ber2]. In this theory classical rigid
L36@P0: spaces are saturated with many new points (analogs of non-closed points of algebraic
L37@P0: varieties), and the obtained spaces are honest topological spaces. In addition,
L38@P0: the obtained topological spaces are rather nice (locally pathwise connected, for
L39@P0: example).
L40@P0-1: 12 MICHAEL TEMKIN
L41@P1: Now, let us list few interesting features of Berkovich theory that distinguish
L42@P1: it from all other approaches. First, one can work with all positive real numbers
L43@P1: almost as well as with the values of |k
L44@P1: ×|. In particular, one can study rings of
L45@P1: power series with radii of convergence linearly independent of |k
L46@P1: ×|. The latter
L47@P1: fact allows to include the case of a trivially valued k into the theory, and the
L48@P1: theory of such k-analytic fields was already applied to classical problems of algebraic
L49@P1: geometry. Another interesting feature is that in a similar fashion one can develop
L50@P1: (an equivalent form of) the usual theory of complex analytic spaces. Moreover, one
L51@P1: can define Berkovich spaces that include both archimedean and non-archimedean
L52@P1: worlds, for example, the affine line over (Z, | |∞).
L53@P1: 1.2. Structure of the notes. We do not aim to prove all results discussed in these
L54@P1: notes (and this is impossible in a six lecture long course). Our goal is to make the
L55@P1: reader familiar with basic definitions, constructions, techniques and results of nonarchimedean analytic geometry. Therefore, we prefer to formulate difficult results
L56@P1: as Facts, and in some cases we discuss main ideas of their proofs in Remarks.
L57@P1: Easy corollaries from these results (that may themselves be important pieces of
L58@P1: the theory) are then suggested as exercises to the reader. Many of exercises are
L59@P1: provided with hints, but it may be worth to first try to solve them independently
L60@P1: (especially, those not marked by an asterisk).
L61@P1: 1.2.1. Overview. The course is divided to five sections as follows. First, we study in
L62@P1: §2 semi-norms, norms and valuations, basic operations with these objects, Banach
L63@P1: rings and their spectra. Then we describe the structure of M(Z), and after that
L64@P1: we switch completely to the non-archimedean world. We finish the section with
L65@P1: describing affine line over an algebraically closed non-archimedean field. In §3 we
L66@P1: introduce k-affinoid algebras and spaces and study their basic properties. In the
L67@P1: next section, this local theory is used to introduce and study global k-analytic
L68@P1: spaces. Relations of k-analytic spaces with other categories are studied in §4. This
L69@P1: includes, analytification of algebraic varieties and GAGA, generic fibers of formal
L70@P1: k
L71@P1: ◦
L72@P1: -schemes and Raynaud’s theory, and some discussion of rigid and adic geometries.
L73@P1: Finally, in §5 we study k-analytic curves in details. In particular, we describe their
L74@P1: local and global structure and explain how this is related to the stable reduction
L75@P1: theorem for formal k
L76@P1: ◦
L77@P1: -curves.
L78@P1: 1.2.2. References and other sources. The main references that helped me to prepare
L79@P1: the course are [Ber1], [Ber2] and [Ber3]. The first two are a book and a large
L80@P1: article in which the non-archimedean analytic spaces were introduced. The third
L81@P1: one is a lecture notes of an analogous introductory course given by Berkovich in
L82@P1: Trieste in 2009. I recommend the third source as an alternative (and shorter)
L83@P1: expositional introductory text. It is worth to note that the first three sections of
L84@P1: [Ber3] and of these notes are parallel, but the exposition is often but not always

L23: 【8†Lemma 9.10.5.】 Let $F$ be a field. Let $\overline{F}$ be an algebraic closure of $F$. Let $M/F$ be an algebraic extension. Then there is a morphism of $F$-extensions $M \to \overline{F}$.
L24: Proof. Consider the set $I$ of pairs $(E, \varphi )$ where $F \subset E \subset M$ is a subextension and $\varphi : E \to \overline{F}$ is a morphism of $F$-extensions. We partially order the set $I$ by declaring $(E, \varphi ) \leq (E', \varphi ')$ if and only if $E \subset E'$ and $\varphi '|_ E = \varphi $. If $T = \{ (E_ t, \varphi _ t)\} \subset I$ is a totally ordered subset, then $\bigcup \varphi _ t : \bigcup E_ t \to \overline{F}$ is an element of $I$.
L25: Thus every totally ordered subset of $I$ has an upper bound. By Zorn's lemma there exists a maximal element $(E, \varphi )$ in $I$. We claim that $E = M$, which will finish the proof. If not, then pick $\alpha \in M$, $\alpha \not\in E$. The $\alpha $ is algebraic over $E$, see Lemma 【15†9.8.4】. Let $P$ be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha $ over $E$. Let $P^\varphi $ be the image of $P$ by $\varphi $ in $\overline{F}[x]$.
L26: Since $\overline{F}$ is algebraically closed there is a root $\beta $ of $P^\varphi $ in $\overline{F}$. Then we can extend $\varphi $ to $\varphi ' : E(\alpha ) = E[x]/(P) \to \overline{F}$ by mapping $x$ to $\beta $. This contradicts the maximality of $(E, \varphi )$ as desired. $\square$

Note that according to Lemma 【15†32.2.3】 we have $X = \mathop{\mathrm{lim}}\nolimits _{i' \geq i} X_{i'}$ and similarly for $Y$.
L42: Since $Y_ i$ and $X_ i$ are of finite presentation over $S_ i$, and since $S_ i$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, also $X_ i$ and $Y_ i$ are quasi-compact and quasi-separated (see Morphisms, Lemma 【16†29.22.10】). Hence we may choose a finite affine open covering $Y_ i = \bigcup V_{j, i}$ such that each $V_{j, i}$ maps into an affine open of $S_ i$. As above, denote $V_{j, i'}$ the inverse image of $V_{j, i}$ in $Y_{i'}$ and $V_ j$ the inverse image in $Y$.
L43: The immersions $V_ j \to Y$ are quasi-compact, and the inverse images $U_ j = \varphi ^{-1}(V_ j)$ are quasi-compact opens of $X$. Hence by Lemma 【17†32.4.11】 there exists an index $i' \geq i$ and quasi-compact opens $U_{j, i'}$ of $X_{i'}$ whose inverse image in $X$ is $U_ j$. Choose an finite affine open covering $U_{j, i'} = \bigcup W_{j, k, i'}$ which induce affine open coverings $U_{j, i''} = \bigcup W_{j, k, i''}$ for all $i'' \geq i'$ and an affine open covering $U_ j = \bigcup W_{j, k}$.
L44: By the affine case there exists an index $i''$ and morphisms $\varphi _{j, k, i''} : W_{j, k, i''} \to V_{j, i''}$ such that $\varphi |_{W_{j, k}} = \varphi _{j, k, i'', S}$ for all $j, k$. By part (3) proved above, there is a further index $i''' \geq i''$ such that
L45: \[ \varphi _{j_1, k_1, i'', S_{i'''}}|_{W_{j_1, k_1, i'''} \cap W_{j_2, k_2, i'''}} = \varphi _{j_2, k_2, i'', S_{i'''}}|_{W_{j_1, k_1, i'''} \cap W_{j_2, k_2, i'''}} \]
L46: 
L47: for all $j_1, j_2, k_1, k_2$. Then $i'''$ is an index such that there exists a morphism $\varphi _{i'''} : X_{i'''} \to Y_{i'''}$ whose base change to $S$ gives $\varphi $. Hence (2) holds.
L48: Let us prove (1). Suppose given a scheme $X$ of finite presentation over $S$. Since $X$ is of finite presentation over $S$, and since $S$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, also $X$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated (see Morphisms, Lemma 【16†29.22.10】). Choose a finite affine open covering $X = \bigcup U_ j$ such that each $U_ j$ maps into an affine open $V_ j \subset S$. Denote $U_{j_1j_2} = U_{j_1} \cap U_{j_2}$ and $U_{j_1j_2j_3} = U_{j_1} \cap U_{j_2} \cap U_{j_3}$.
L49: By Lemmas 【17†32.4.11】 and 【18†32.4.13】 we can find an index $i_1$ and affine opens $V_{j, i_1} \subset S_{i_1}$ such that each $V_ j$ is the inverse of this in $S$. Let $V_{j, i}$ be the inverse image of $V_{j, i_1}$ in $S_ i$ for $i \geq i_1$. By the affine case we may find an index $i_2 \geq i_1$ and affine schemes $U_{j, i_2} \to V_{j, i_2}$ such that $U_ j = S \times _{S_{i_2}} U_{j, i_2}$ is the base change. Denote $U_{j, i} = S_ i \times _{S_{i_2}} U_{j, i_2}$ for $i \geq i_2$.
L50: By Lemma 【17†32.4.11】 there exists an index $i_3 \geq i_2$ and open subschemes $W_{j_1, j_2, i_3} \subset U_{j_1, i_3}$ whose base change to $S$ is equal to $U_{j_1j_2}$. Denote $W_{j_1, j_2, i} = S_ i \times _{S_{i_3}} W_{j_1, j_2, i_3}$ for $i \geq i_3$. By part (2) shown above there exists an index $i_4 \geq i_3$ and morphisms $\varphi _{j_1, j_2, i_4} : W_{j_1, j_2, i_4} \to W_{j_2, j_1, i_4}$ whose base change to $S$ gives the identity morphism $U_{j_1j_2} = U_{j_2j_1}$ for all $j_1, j_2$.
L51: For all $i \geq i_4$ denote $\varphi _{j_1, j_2, i} = \text{id}_ S \times \varphi _{j_1, j_2, i_4}$ the base change. We claim that for some $i_5 \geq i_4$ the system $((U_{j, i_5})_ j, (W_{j_1, j_2, i_5})_{j_1, j_2}, (\varphi _{j_1, j_2, i_5})_{j_1, j_2})$ forms a glueing datum as in Schemes, Section 【19†26.14】. In order to see this we have to verify that for $i$ large enough we have
L52: \[ \varphi _{j_1, j_2, i}^{-1}(W_{j_2, j_1, i} \cap W_{j_2, j_3, i}) = W_{j_1, j_2, i} \cap W_{j_1, j_3, i} \]
L53: and that for large enough $i$ the cocycle condition holds. The first condition follows from Lemma 【17†32.4.11】 and the fact that $U_{j_2j_1j_3} = U_{j_1j_2j_3}$. The second from part (3) of the lemma proved above and the fact that the cocycle condition holds for the maps $\text{id} : U_{j_1j_2} \to U_{j_2j_1}$. Ok, so now we can use Schemes, Lemma 【20†26.14.2】 to glue the system $((U_{j, i_5})_ j, (W_{j_1, j_2, i_5})_{j_1, j_2}, (\varphi _{j_1, j_2, i_5})_{j_1, j_2})$ to get a scheme $X_{i_5} \to S_{i_5}$.
L54: By construction the base change of $X_{i_5}$ to $S$ is formed by glueing the open affines $U_ j$ along the opens $U_{j_1} \leftarrow U_{j_1j_2} \rightarrow U_{j_2}$. Hence $S \times _{S_{i_5}} X_{i_5} \cong X$ as desired. $\square$

L23: 【8†Lemma 32.10.2.】 Let $I$ be a directed set. Let $(S_ i, f_{ii'})$ be an inverse system of schemes over $I$. Assume
L24: 
L25:   1. all the morphisms $f_{ii'} : S_ i \to S_{i'}$ are affine,
L26: 
L27:   2. all the schemes $S_ i$ are quasi-compact and quasi-separated.
L28: 
L29: Let $S = \mathop{\mathrm{lim}}\nolimits _ i S_ i$. Then we have the following:
L30:   1. For any sheaf of $\mathcal{O}_ S$-modules $\mathcal{F}$ of finite presentation there exists an index $i \in I$ and a sheaf of $\mathcal{O}_{S_ i}$-modules of finite presentation $\mathcal{F}_ i$ such that $\mathcal{F} \cong f_ i^*\mathcal{F}_ i$.
L31:   2. Suppose given an index $i \in I$, sheaves of $\mathcal{O}_{S_ i}$-modules $\mathcal{F}_ i$, $\mathcal{G}_ i$ of finite presentation and a morphism $\varphi : f_ i^*\mathcal{F}_ i \to f_ i^*\mathcal{G}_ i$ over $S$. Then there exists an index $i' \geq i$ and a morphism $\varphi _{i'} : f_{i'i}^*\mathcal{F}_ i \to f_{i'i}^*\mathcal{G}_ i$ whose base change to $S$ is $\varphi $.
L32:   3. Suppose given an index $i \in I$, sheaves of $\mathcal{O}_{S_ i}$-modules $\mathcal{F}_ i$, $\mathcal{G}_ i$ of finite presentation and a pair of morphisms $\varphi _ i, \psi _ i : \mathcal{F}_ i \to \mathcal{G}_ i$. Assume that the base changes are equal: $f_ i^*\varphi _ i = f_ i^*\psi _ i$. Then there exists an index $i' \geq i$ such that $f_{i'i}^*\varphi _ i = f_{i'i}^*\psi _ i$.
L33: In other words, the category of modules of finite presentation over $S$ is the colimit over $I$ of the categories modules of finite presentation over $S_ i$.
L34: 
L35: Proof. We sketch two proofs, but we omit the details.
L36: 
L37: First proof. If $S$ and $S_ i$ are affine schemes, then this lemma is equivalent to Algebra, Lemma 【15†10.127.6】. In the general case, use Zariski glueing to deduce it from the affine case.
L38: 
L39: Second proof. We use
L40:   1. there is an equivalence of categories between quasi-coherent $\mathcal{O}_ S$-modules and vector bundles over $S$, see Constructions, Section 【16†27.6】, and
L41: 
L42:   2. a vector bundle $\mathbf{V}(\mathcal{F}) \to S$ is of finite presentation over $S$ if and only if $\mathcal{F}$ is an $\mathcal{O}_ S$-module of finite presentation.
L43: Having said this, we can use Lemma 【10†32.10.1】 to show that the category of vector bundles of finite presentation over $S$ is the colimit over $I$ of the categories of vector bundles over $S_ i$. $\square$

L22: 【8†Lemma 74.13.1.】 Let $S$ be a scheme. Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism of algebraic spaces over $S$. Let $\mathcal{L}$ be an invertible $\mathcal{O}_ X$-module. Let $\{ g_ i : Y_ i \to Y\} _{i \in I}$ be an fpqc covering. Let $f_ i : X_ i \to Y_ i$ be the base change of $f$ and let $\mathcal{L}_ i$ be the pullback of $\mathcal{L}$ to $X_ i$. The following are equivalent
L23: 
L24:   1. $\mathcal{L}$ is ample on $X/Y$, and
L25: 
L26:   2. $\mathcal{L}_ i$ is ample on $X_ i/Y_ i$ for every $i \in I$.
L27: Proof. The implication (1) $\Rightarrow $ (2) follows from Divisors on Spaces, Lemma 【14†71.14.3】. Assume (2). To check $\mathcal{L}$ is ample on $X/Y$ we may work étale locally on $Y$, see Divisors on Spaces, Lemma 【15†71.14.6】. Thus we may assume that $Y$ is a scheme and then we may in turn assume each $Y_ i$ is a scheme too, see Topologies on Spaces, Lemma 【16†73.9.5】. In other words, we may assume that $\{ Y_ i \to Y\} $ is an fpqc covering of schemes.
L28: By Divisors on Spaces, Lemma 【17†71.14.4】 we see that $X_ i \to Y_ i$ is representable (i.e., $X_ i$ is a scheme), quasi-compact, and separated. Hence $f$ is quasi-compact and separated by Lemmas 【18†74.11.1】 and 【19†74.11.18】. This means that $\mathcal{A} = \bigoplus _{d \geq 0} f_*\mathcal{L}^{\otimes d}$ is a quasi-coherent graded $\mathcal{O}_ Y$-algebra (Morphisms of Spaces, Lemma 【20†67.11.2】).
L29: Moreover, the formation of $\mathcal{A}$ commutes with flat base change by Cohomology of Spaces, Lemma 【21†69.11.2】. In particular, if we set $\mathcal{A}_ i = \bigoplus _{d \geq 0} f_{i, *}\mathcal{L}_ i^{\otimes d}$ then we have $\mathcal{A}_ i = g_ i^*\mathcal{A}$.
L30: It follows that the natural maps $\psi _ d : f^*\mathcal{A}_ d \to \mathcal{L}^{\otimes d}$ of $\mathcal{O}_ X$ pullback to give the natural maps $\psi _{i, d} : f_ i^*(\mathcal{A}_ i)_ d \to \mathcal{L}_ i^{\otimes d}$ of $\mathcal{O}_{X_ i}$-modules. Since $\mathcal{L}_ i$ is ample on $X_ i/Y_ i$ we see that for any point $x_ i \in X_ i$, there exists a $d \geq 1$ such that $f_ i^*(\mathcal{A}_ i)_ d \to \mathcal{L}_ i^{\otimes d}$ is surjective on stalks at $x_ i$.
L31: This follows either directly from the definition of a relatively ample module or from Morphisms, Lemma 【22†29.38.4】. If $x \in |X|$, then we can choose an $i$ and an $x_ i \in X_ i$ mapping to $x$. Since $\mathcal{O}_{X, \overline{x}} \to \mathcal{O}_{X_ i, \overline{x}_ i}$ is flat hence faithfully flat, we conclude that for every $x \in |X|$ there exists a $d \geq 1$ such that $f^*\mathcal{A}_ d \to \mathcal{L}^{\otimes d}$ is surjective on stalks at $x$.
L32: This implies that the open subset $U(\psi ) \subset X$ of Divisors on Spaces, Lemma 【23†71.13.1】 corresponding to the map $\psi : f^*\mathcal{A} \to \bigoplus _{d \geq 0} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes d}$ of graded $\mathcal{O}_ X$-algebras is equal to $X$. Consider the corresponding morphism
L33: \[ r_{\mathcal{L}, \psi } : X \longrightarrow \underline{\text{Proj}}_ Y(\mathcal{A}) \]
L34: 
L35: It is clear from the above that the base change of $r_{\mathcal{L}, \psi }$ to $Y_ i$ is the morphism $r_{\mathcal{L}_ i, \psi _ i}$ which is an open immersion by Morphisms, Lemma 【22†29.38.4】. Hence $r_{\mathcal{L}, \psi }$ is an open immersion by Lemma 【24†74.11.14】. Hence $X$ is a scheme and we conclude $\mathcal{L}$ is ample on $X/Y$ by Morphisms, Lemma 【22†29.38.4】. $\square$

1.4. Integrally closed test configurations and divisorial valuations.
Definition 1.10. We say that a test configuration X for X is integrally closed if the scheme
X is integrally closed in the generic fiber Xk($) of π : X → A1 .
  In other words, X is integrally closed iff it can be covered by affine open subsets U =
Spec A such that the k[$]-algebra A is integrally closed in Ak($) . Note that X is normal iff
X is normal and X is integrally closed.
Example 1.11. The trivial test configuration Xtriv = X × A1 is integrally closed.
   The integral closure of any test configuration X in Xk($) defines a finite, Gm -equivariant
morphism Xe → X (because the scheme X , being of finite type over a field, is excellent),
which induces an isomorphism on the generic fibers over A1 . Thus Xe is an integrally closed
test configuration for X, which we simply call the integral closure of X . It is characterized
as the unique integrally closed test configuration that dominates X via a finite morphism.
   When X is normal, the integral closure Xe of any test configuration X coincides with its
normalization X ν (see also Remark 1.22).
Lemma 1.12 (Zariski’s main theorem). If X is integrally closed and µ : X 0 → X is a
morphism of test configurations, then µ? OX 0 = OX .
Proof. By coherence of direct images, µ? OX 0 is a finite OX -module. Sections of µ? OX 0 on
an open U ⊂ X are thus rational functions on U that are regular on the generic fiber and
integral over OU , and hence belong to OU .                                                
  Integral closedness admits the following characterization, a ‘vertical version’ of the usual
Serre criterion for normality.
Theorem 1.13. A test configuration X is integrally closed iff it is:
   (i) vertically R1 , in the sense that X is regular at each generic points of X0 ;
  (ii) vertically S2 , in the sense that depth OX ,ξ ≥ min{2, dim OX ,ξ } for all ξ ∈ X0 .
Remark 1.14. Condition (i) was called partially normal in [Oda13, Definition 3.7].
Lemma 1.15. For any test configuration X for X, we have:
   (i) X is vertically S2 ⇐⇒ X0 is S1 , i.e. without embedded points;
  (ii) X is S2 ⇐⇒ X is S2 and X is vertically S2 .
              GLOBAL PLURIPOTENTIAL THEORY OVER A TRIVIALLY VALUED FIELD                       17

Proof. Since X0 is a Cartier divisor, each ξ ∈ X0 satisfies
                depth OX ,ξ = depth OX0 ,ξ + 1,    dim OX ,ξ = dim OX0 ,ξ + 1.
This yields (i), while (ii) is a direct consequence of the isomorphism
                                      X \ X0 ≃ X × Gm .
                                                                                              
Corollary 1.16. For any test configuration X , the following are equivalent:
   (i) X0 is reduced;
  (ii) X is integrally closed, and X0 is generically reduced.
Proof. The scheme X0 is reduced iff it is generically reduced and S1 . By Lemma 1.15, X0
is thus reduced iff it is generically reduced and X is vertically S2 . Finally, X0 generically
reduced implies that X is regular at each generic point of X0 , since the latter is a Cartier
divisor. The result is now a consequence of Theorem 1.13.                                   
  Before entering the proof of Theorem 1.13, we introduce some terminology that will be
used throughout this paper.
Definition 1.17. Let X be a test configuration for X.
    (i) A vertical fractional ideal a on X is a coherent fractional ideal sheaf that is Gm -
        invariant, and trivial outside X0 .
   (ii) The polar scheme P ⊂ X of a vertical fractional ideal a is the closed subscheme of
        X defined by the ideal of poles p := {f ∈ OX | f a ⊂ OX }.
  (iii) A vertical Cartier divisor D on X is a Gm -invariant Cartier divisor with support in
        X0 .
   Note that P in (ii) is supported in X0 , a being trivial outside X0 .
   Vertical Cartier divisors on X are in 1–1 correspondence with locally principal vertical
fractional ideals of X , via D 7→ OX (D). If D is further effective, then it coincides with the
polar scheme of OX (D).
Lemma 1.18. A test configuration X is integrally closed iff every vertical fractional ideal

L23: 【8†Lemma 33.27.4.】 Let $k$ be a field. Let $X$ be an algebraic $k$-scheme. Then there exists a finite purely inseparable extension $k'/k$ such that the normalization $Y$ of $X_{k'}$ is geometrically normal over $k'$.
L24: Proof. Let $K = k^{perf}$ be the perfect closure. Let $Y_ K$ be the normalization of $X_ K$, see Lemma 【15†33.27.1】. By Limits, Lemma 【16†32.10.1】 there exists a finite sub extension $K/k'/k$ and a morphism $\nu : Y \to X_{k'}$ of finite presentation whose base change to $K$ is the normalization morphism $\nu _ K : Y_ K \to X_ K$. Observe that $Y$ is geometrically normal over $k'$ (Lemma 【17†33.10.3】). After increasing $k'$ we may assume $Y \to X_{k'}$ is finite (Limits, Lemma 【18†32.8.3】).
L25: Since $\nu _ K : Y_ K \to X_ K$ is the normalization morphism, it induces a birational morphism $Y_ K \to (X_ K)_{red}$. Hence there is a dense open $V_ K \subset X_ K$ such that $\nu _ K^{-1}(V_ K) \to V_ K$ is a closed immersion (inducing an isomorphism of $\nu _ K^{-1}(V_ K)$ with $V_{K, red}$, see for example Morphisms, Lemma 【19†29.52.6】).
L26: After increasing $k'$ we find $V_ K$ is the base change of a dense open $V \subset Y$ and the morphism $\nu ^{-1}(V) \to V$ is a closed immersion (Limits, Lemmas 【20†32.4.11】 and 【21†32.8.5】). It follows readily from this that $\nu $ is the normalization morphism and the proof is complete. $\square$

L23: 【8†Lemma 10.112.8.】 Let $R \to S$ be a local homomorphism of local Noetherian rings. Assume
L24:

Then we see that $x_1, \ldots , x_ d, y_1, \ldots , y_ e$ are elements which generate the maximal ideal of $S$ and $e + d = \dim (S)$. $\square$

L22: 【8†Lemma 10.110.9.】 Let $R \to S$ be a local homomorphism of local Noetherian rings. Assume that $R \to S$ is flat and that $S$ is regular. Then $R$ is regular.
L23: Proof. Let $\mathfrak m \subset R$ be the maximal ideal and let $\kappa = R/\mathfrak m$ be the residue field. Let $d = \dim S$. Choose any resolution $F_\bullet \to \kappa $ with each $F_ i$ a finite free $R$-module. Set $K_ d = \mathop{\mathrm{Ker}}(F_{d - 1} \to F_{d - 2})$. By flatness of $R \to S$ the complex $0 \to K_ d \otimes _ R S \to F_{d - 1} \otimes _ R S \to \ldots \to F_0 \otimes _ R S \to \kappa \otimes _ R S \to 0$ is still exact.
L24: Because the global dimension of $S$ is $d$, see Proposition 【14†10.110.1】, we see that $K_ d \otimes _ R S$ is a finite free $S$-module (see also Lemma 【15†10.109.3】). By Lemma 【16†10.78.6】 we see that $K_ d$ is a finite free $R$-module. Hence $\kappa $ has finite projective dimension and $R$ is regular by Proposition 【17†10.110.5】. $\square$

premises.statement: For a projective finite-presentation flat family and a finitely presented flat sheaf, Euler characteristics are locally constant; generic flatness and generic geometric integrality permit shrinking a finite-type integral field-of-definition base. These apply separately to a fixed curve and fixed line bundle.

Proposition 5.13 extends a projective morphism on a flat schematic graph model and identifies pulled model metrics. premises.statement: Temkin defines multipointed curves as flat finitely presented schemes with pure one-dimensional fibers. A multipointed curve over integral qcqs S with semistable generic fiber has a stable modification after generically etale alteration. Stable modification morphisms are projective. Proposition 4.5.1 proves the valuation-ring application for separably closed valued fields of finite height.
